paragraphs.title: Trusting Egypt Is No Substitute for Trusting God

easy.explanation: The verse begins, “Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help.”
easy.q: Where do the people go for help?

easy.explanation: They trusted in horses, chariots, and strong horsemen.
easy.q: What did the people trust in?

answers: The Holy One of Israel and the Lord
easy.explanation: They “look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the Lord.”
easy.q: Whom did they fail to seek?

answers: The Egyptians are men, and not God
medium.explanation: The passage says, “The Egyptians are men, and not God.”
medium.q: Why is Egypt not a reliable source of salvation?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “both he that helpeth shall fall, and he that is holpen shall fall down.”
medium.q: What will happen to the helper and the one being helped?

answers: They did not turn to or rely upon
medium.explanation: The people did not turn to God for guidance and help.
medium.q: What does the phrase “look not unto” mean in this passage?

answers: Between human strength and the power of God
challenge.explanation: Human military power is contrasted with the wisdom and power of God.
challenge.q: What major contrast is presented in these verses?

answers: The Lord acts wisely and fulfills His word
challenge.explanation: The Lord will bring evil and “will not call back his words,” showing that His word stands.
challenge.q: What does the statement “he also is wise” teach about the Lord?

answers: They represent reliance on military strength instead of God
They prove that Egypt is not human
challenge.explanation: The military forces show the people's misplaced confidence in human power.
challenge.q: Why does the passage emphasize horses, chariots, and horsemen?

easy.explanation: The Lord will come down to fight for Mount Zion and its hill.
easy.q: Where will the Lord of hosts come down to fight?

answers: A lion and a young lion
easy.explanation: The Lord is compared to a lion and a young lion that are not afraid of shepherds.
easy.q: What animal is used to describe the Lord's courage against His enemies?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “so will the Lord of hosts defend Jerusalem.”

answers: He is frightened by their noise
He is not afraid of them
medium.explanation: Like a lion that is not afraid of the shepherds' voice, the Lord is not intimidated.
medium.q: What does the lion image show about the Lord's response to His enemies?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “defending also he will deliver it; and passing over he will preserve it.”
medium.q: Which acts of protection are named in verse 5?

answers: Moving over the city to preserve it
medium.explanation: The phrase describes the Lord's protective action over Jerusalem.
medium.q: What does “passing over” suggest in the context of protecting Jerusalem?

answers: Both portray the Lord as a fearless protector
Both explain how Jerusalem's walls were built
challenge.explanation: The lion shows courage, while the birds show active protection and preservation.
challenge.q: What connection exists between the lion and bird images?

answers: The Lord leaves Zion and then returns
The Lord confronts the threat and then protects Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: The Lord comes to fight for Zion and then defends, delivers, and preserves Jerusalem.
challenge.q: What sequence of ideas appears in verses 4–5?

answers: The Lord's dependence on human armies
challenge.explanation: The image presents the Lord as actively sheltering and preserving Jerusalem.
challenge.q: What does the image of birds flying emphasize?

paragraphs.title: A Call to Return and Reject Idolatry

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Turn ye unto him from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted.”
easy.q: To whom is the command “Turn ye” addressed?

easy.explanation: They are called to return from their deep rebellion against the Lord.
easy.q: From what are the people called to turn?

answers: Their idols of silver and gold
easy.explanation: They will cast away their idols of silver and gold.
easy.q: What will people cast away in that day?

answers: The call to return leads to rejecting idols
Rejecting idols leads to seeking Egypt
Jerusalem's protection removes the call to return
medium.explanation: After calling Israel to return, the passage says they will cast away their idols.
medium.q: What is the relationship between verses 6 and 7?

medium.explanation: The verse calls them idols “which your own hands have made unto you for a sin.”
medium.q: Who made the silver and golden idols?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes serious and deep rebellion against the Lord.

answers: It connects God's protection with the need for Israel to return to Him
It shows that God will not protect Jerusalem
It presents Egypt as the true deliverer
challenge.explanation: Because the Lord protects His people, they are urged to abandon rebellion and return to Him.
challenge.q: Why does the call to return follow the description of God's protection?

answers: They gave divine honor to things they themselves created
The idols were sent from Egypt
challenge.explanation: The passage exposes the foolishness of worshiping objects made by human hands.
challenge.q: What is significant about the idols being made by the people's own hands?

answers: A time when God's power is revealed and idols are rejected
A day when Egypt sends horses
challenge.explanation: The phrase points to the time when the people will cast away their idols.
challenge.q: What does “in that day” indicate in the flow of the passage?

paragraphs.title: Assyria's Fall by a Power Beyond Humanity

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Then shall the Assyrian fall.”

answers: A sword wielded by an ordinary man
A sword not of a human warrior
easy.explanation: The Assyrian will fall by a sword “not of a mighty man” and “not of a mean man.”
easy.q: By what kind of sword will Assyria fall?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “his young men shall be discomfited.”
easy.q: What will happen to the young men of Assyria?

medium.explanation: The passage says, “he shall flee from the sword.”
medium.q: What will the Assyrian do because of the sword?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “his princes shall be afraid of the ensign.”
medium.q: What will happen to the princes of Assyria?

medium.explanation: The Assyrian young men will be overcome and put into disorder.
medium.q: What does “discomfited” mean in this passage?

answers: Assyria's defeat will not be achieved by ordinary human power
challenge.explanation: The wording points to a power beyond normal human strength.
challenge.q: What does the repeated contrast with human warriors emphasize?

answers: Assyria retreats while God's presence remains in Zion and Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: Assyria is terrified, while the Lord's fire and furnace remain in Zion and Jerusalem.
challenge.q: How does verse 9 connect with the protection described earlier?

answers: Assyria is stronger than God and cannot fall
Assyria retreats in fear while Jerusalem is associated with God's protecting presence
Egypt replaces Assyria as Jerusalem's protector
challenge.explanation: The ending contrasts Assyria's fear and retreat with the Lord's fire in Zion and Jerusalem.
challenge.q: What overall picture is presented at the end of the chapter?
